abstract: Intermittent fasting (IF) is increasingly recognized as a potent modulator of metabolic health, but its effects on brain function across generations remain poorly understood. Here, we show that parental IF, administered to both mothers and fathers before mating, is associated with coordinated molecular remodeling in the cerebral cortex of fathers and their offspring, with shared molecular signatures identified between these generations and a pronounced enrichment of sensory-associated pathways. Using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, transcriptomic profiling, and proteomic analysis, we found that IF elicited widespread cortical epigenetic remodeling in fathers, accompanied by transcriptional and protein-level changes enriched for olfactory, taste, synaptic, and neurometabolic pathways. Strikingly, related molecular signatures were detected in F1 offspring that had never been directly exposed to fasting, consistent with intergenerational transmission of IF-associated cortical remodeling. Offspring responses were sex dependent, with female and male progeny exhibiting distinct patterns of DNA methylation, gene expression, and protein abundance. Integrated multiomic analyses identified conserved candidate networks involved in sensory perception, glutamatergic signaling, synaptic organization, intracellular trafficking, cytoskeletal regulation, and stress-response pathways. Together, these findings identify sensory-associated cortical remodeling as a prominent molecular feature associated with parental IF and reveal persistent, sex-dependent molecular alterations in the offspring brain.
